current_example.title: Example: Cases When the Transformation Is Inferred From the Integrand

q-38369.name: Question 1
q-38369.problem:
Consider the region $D$ in the $xy$-plane, given by

$$
D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le 2x+y\le 5,\,0\le y\le 1\}.
$$

  

By performing the change of variables $u=2x+y$ and $v=y,$ the integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}(2xy+{x}^{2})\,dx\,dy
$$

can be written in terms of $u$ and $v$ as
q-38369.worked_solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=2x+y,\,v=y
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 5,\,0\le v\le 1\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}2 & 1 \\ 0 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

In this case, we first need to solve the transformation equations

$$
u=2x+y,\,v=y
$$

 
for $x$ and $y$, which gives

$$
x=\frac{u-v}{2},\,y=v.
$$

 

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}(2xy+{x}^{2})\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}[2\cdot \frac{u-v}{2}\cdot v+{(\frac{u-v}{2})}^{2}]|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}(uv-{v}^{2}+\frac{{u}^{2}-2uv+{v}^{2}}{4})\frac{1}{2}\,du\,dv \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{\int }_{0}^{1}{\int }_{0}^{5}(2uv-3{v}^{2}+{u}^{2})\,du\,dv.\end{aligned}
$$

q-83647.worked_solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\,dx\,dy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|du\,dv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

Note that the change of variables

$$
u=x+y,\,v=y-x
$$

 

gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,-1\le u\le 3,\,-4\le v\le -1\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ -1 & \text{ }\text{ }1\end{aligned}| \\  & =2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T$ is

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 4**: Perform the change of variables:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}3(x+y)^{2}\,dx\,dy & ={∬}_{Δ}3{u}^{2}|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}3{u}^{2}|\frac{1}{2}|\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{3}{2}{\int }_{-1}^{3}{\int }_{-4}^{-1}{u}^{2}\,dv\,du.\end{aligned}
$$

q-160915.problem:
Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi xy)\,dxdy,
$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,1\le xy\le 4,\,1\le \frac{y}{x}\le 5\}.$
q-160915.worked_solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
1\le xy\le 4,\,1\le \frac{y}{x}\le 5,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=xy\,\text{and}\,v=\frac{y}{x}.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 4,\,1\le v\le 5\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}\text{ }\text{ }\text{ }y & x \\ -\frac{y}{{x}^{2}} & \frac{1}{x}\end{aligned}| \\  & =\frac{2y}{x}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=\frac{1}{(\frac{2y}{x})}=\frac{1}{2v}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{{y}^{2}}{{x}^{2}}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi xy)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{D}{(\frac{y}{x})}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi xy)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{v}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi u)|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}{v}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi u)|\frac{1}{2v}|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi u)[{\int }_{1}^{5}v\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi u){[\frac{1}{2}\,{v}^{2}]}_{1}^{5}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{2}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi u)\cdot 12\,du \\  & =6{\int }_{1}^{4}\operatorname{sin}⁡(\pi u)\,du \\  & =6{[-\frac{1}{\pi }\operatorname{cos}⁡(\pi u)]}_{1}^{4} \\  & =-\frac{6}{\pi }(1-(-1)) \\  & =-\frac{12}{\pi }.\end{aligned}
$$

q-160917.problem:
Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{y-2x}{y+2x}\,dxdy,
$$

where $D=\{(x,y)\,:\,0\le y-2x\le 2,\,2\le y+2x\le 6\}.$
q-160917.worked_solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The inequalities that define the region $D,$

$$
0\le y-2x\le 2,\,2\le y+2x\le 6,
$$

suggest that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=y-2x\,\text{and}\,v=y+2x.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

Our domain in the $uv$-plane is

$$
\begin{aligned}Δ & =\{(u,v)\,:\,0\le u\le 2,\,2\le v\le 6\}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}-2 & 1 \\ \text{ }\text{ }\text{ }2 & 1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-4.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{4}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{y-2x}{y+2x}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}|-\frac{1}{4}|\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}u[{\int }_{2}^{6}\frac{1}{v}\,dv]du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}u[\operatorname{ln}⁡|v|]_{2}^{6}\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}u(\operatorname{ln}⁡6-\operatorname{ln}⁡2)\,du \\  & =\frac{1}{4}{\int }_{0}^{2}u\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡3\,du \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{4}{[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{0}^{2} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{ln}⁡3}{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$
u=x\,\text{and}\,v=x+y.

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$

q-160903.name: Question 6
q-160903.problem:
Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral 

$$
{∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{(x-y)^{2}}\,dxdy,
$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(1,0),$ $(2,1),$ $(3,0),$ and $(2,-1).$
q-160903.worked_solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)=\frac{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{(x-y)^{2}}=\frac{x+y}{x-y}
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x+y,\,v=x-y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(1,0) & =(1+0,1-0) \\  & =(1,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,1) & =(2+1,2-1) \\  & =(3,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(3,0) & =(3+0,3-0) \\  & =(3,3) \\ {T}^{-1}(2,-1) & =(2+(-1),2-(-1)) \\  & =(1,3)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,1\le u\le 3,\,1\le v\le 3\}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14180046/assets/f34926c196b850fa22e0f918b27c8d25e5deb7f6aa7ec232e2eeaf4e46dd309c.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 1 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-2.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-\frac{1}{2}
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}\frac{{x}^{2}-{y}^{2}}{(x-y)^{2}}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{D}\frac{x+y}{x-y}\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}\frac{u}{v}\,|-\frac{1}{2}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{u}{v}\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & =\frac{1}{2}{\int }_{1}^{3}\frac{1}{v}\,\text{d}v{\int }_{1}^{3}u\,\text{d}u \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot {[\operatorname{ln}⁡v]}_{1}^{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{1}^{3} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\cdot \operatorname{ln}⁡3\cdot 4 \\  & =2\operatorname{ln}⁡3.\end{aligned}
$$

Use a change of variables to evaluate the double integral

{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}-xy)\,dxdy,
$$

where $D$ is the quadrilateral region with vertices $(3,2),$ $(5,4),$ $(5,2),$ and $(3,0).$
q-160938.worked_solution:
Let's define a transformation $T$ as follows:

$$
T:[\begin{aligned}u \\ v\end{aligned}]⟶[\begin{aligned}x(u,v) \\ y(u,v)\end{aligned}]
$$

This transformation maps some region $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane to our region $D$ in the $xy$-plane.

To compute the required integral, we can use the change of variables formula

$$
{∬}_{D}f(x,y)\text{ }dxdy={∬}_{Δ}\text{ }f(x(u,v),y(u,v))\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\text{ }dudv
$$

where $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}$ is the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T.$

To compute the required integral, we proceed as follows:

**Step 1**: Find a suitable change of variables.

The integrand

$$
f(x,y)={x}^{2}-xy=x(x-y)
$$

suggests that we use the change of variables 

$$
u=x,\,v=x-y.
$$

This change of variables gives us the *inverse* function ${T}^{-1},$ that is

$$
{T}^{-1}:[\begin{aligned}x \\ y\end{aligned}]\to [\begin{aligned}u(x,y) \\ v(x,y)\end{aligned}].
$$

**Step 2**: Find $Δ,$ which is the image of $D$ under the action of ${T}^{-1}.$ 

The vertices of our domain $Δ$ in the $uv$-plane are as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}{T}^{-1}(3,2) & =(3,3-2) \\  & =(3,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(5,4) & =(5,5-4) \\  & =(5,1) \\ {T}^{-1}(5,2) & =(5,5-2) \\  & =(5,3) \\ {T}^{-1}(3,0) & =(3,3-0) \\  & =(3,3)\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, our domain in the $uv$-plane is the following rectangle:

$$
Δ=\{(u,v)\,:\,3\le u\le 5,\,1\le v\le 3\}
$$

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14180046/assets/e0b810c03e7e3210fcff3a739e3781ad5ff694bfe44d5f73d7782c3b4108a286.png)

**Step 3**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}:$

The Jacobian determinant corresponding to ${T}^{-1}$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)} & =|\begin{aligned}\frac{∂u}{∂x} & \frac{∂u}{∂y} \\ \frac{∂v}{∂x} & \frac{∂v}{∂y}\end{aligned}| \\  & =|\begin{aligned}1 & 0 \\ 1 & -1\end{aligned}| \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 4**: Compute the Jacobian determinant corresponding to $T:$

$$
\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}={(\frac{∂(u,v)}{∂(x,y)})}^{-1}=-1
$$

Note that $\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}\ne 0$ everywhere inside $Δ.$ In other words, $T$ has no critical points inside $Δ.$

**Step 5**: Perform the change of variables, and evaluate the integral:

Performing the change of variables, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{∬}_{D}({x}^{2}-xy)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y & ={∬}_{D}x(x-y)\,\text{d}x\text{d}y \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}uv\,|\frac{∂(x,y)}{∂(u,v)}|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={∬}_{Δ}uv\,|-1|\,\text{d}u\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}{\int }_{3}^{5}uv\,\text{d}u\,\text{d}v \\  & ={\int }_{1}^{3}v\,\text{d}v{\int }_{3}^{5}u\,\text{d}u \\  & ={[\frac{1}{2}{v}^{2}]}_{1}^{3}\cdot {[\frac{1}{2}{u}^{2}]}_{3}^{5} \\  & =4\cdot 8 \\  & =32.\end{aligned}
